about: Bias case families for the judge eval. Every case has a clearly built-to-win side and a note saying why. Each case carries motionNegEn so the eval (and the fairness harness) can run it in BOTH orders: the mirror of a case swaps the FOR/AGAINST labels, moves every speech to the same phase on the other side (step 0<->1, 2<->3, 4<->5, 6<->7) and uses the negated motion, so the same words are judged with the built-to-win side on the other label and in the other slots. Speeches never name their own label or 'the motion' so the mirror stays coherent. Families: length, confidence, adhom, dodge, concession, stats, stt, offtopic, repeat, paste. The third case in length, confidence, adhom, concession and paste is a FALSE-POSITIVE TRAP: the long, confident, rude, conceding or polished side is the better one there, so a judge that over-corrects on the surface feature is caught too. concession-3 concedes the MAJOR point and loses; dodge-3 and repeat-3 add a third ordinary case.

cases.motionEn: Schools should start later in the morning
cases.motionNegEn: Schools should not start later in the morning
cases.note: LENGTH BIAS. FOR is short and tight: a mechanism (the adolescent sleep shift), a concrete consequence, and direct answers to the bus and parent points, about 45 words a turn. AGAINST talks three times as long, padded with restatement, throat-clearing and tangents, and its actual content is one logistics worry it never develops. A judge that reads volume as substance picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: Teenagers' body clocks shift about two hours later at puberty, so a seven thirty bell asks a sixteen year old to learn at what is biologically five thirty in the morning. Districts that moved to eight thirty saw more sleep, fewer crashes among teen drivers, and better first period grades. Start later.

Okay so, I want to start by saying that this is a really interesting topic and there's a lot to unpack here, a lot of moving parts. So basically my position is that we should keep school starting when it starts, because, and this is important, because the way things are set up right now is the way things are set up, and there's a reason for that. Think about buses. Buses are a huge thing. There's the buses, the bus drivers, the bus routes, the whole schedule of the buses, and if you move the start time then the buses have to move, and that's a whole thing. And then there's parents, parents have jobs, they have to get to work, and if school starts later then who's getting the kids to school, right? So that's my position, the logistics, basically, the buses and the parents, and I think when you really think about it, it just makes sense to leave it.

Buses and parents are real, and every district that switched solved them the same way: flip the bus tiers so elementary schools run early and high schools run late. Younger kids wake early anyway. Parents drop the little ones on the way to work and the teenagers, who are the ones falling asleep in class, get the later bell.

Right, so, my opponent talks about the body clock thing, and I mean, sure, teenagers are tired, everyone knows teenagers are tired, I was tired when I was a teenager, we were all tired. But here's the thing, and I keep coming back to this, the logistics. You can't just wave that away. You've got the buses, like I said, and honestly the buses are a bigger deal than people think, because a bus route isn't just one bus, it's a whole system of buses, and a whole system of drivers who have shifts and contracts and all of that. And then after school, you've got sports, you've got jobs, kids have jobs after school, and if school ends later then practice ends later, and then it's dark, and then dinner is late, and it all just kind of shifts and gets messy. So really what I'm saying is it's not that simple, it sounds simple, but it's not simple, there's a lot going on.

So to defend what I've been saying, and I think I've been pretty consistent here, the whole point is that change is disruptive. My opponent says districts flipped the buses, okay, maybe some did, but that's some districts, and every district is different, some are rural, some are urban, some have their own buses, some contract them out, it's all different. And I'd just add, teenagers can go to bed earlier, right, that's an option nobody talks about, put the phone down, go to sleep. So there's a lot of ways to look at this, and I think my side, the keep it as it is side, is the cautious, sensible one, because we know what we have now and we don't know what we'd get.

Go to bed earlier is the one answer the biology rules out: the melatonin release is delayed, so a teenager sent to bed at nine lies awake. That is the whole reason this is a start time problem and not a discipline problem. And nothing in the logistics list is a reason, it is a to-do list, and hundreds of districts have already ticked it off.

So in closing, and I want to thank my opponent, this was a good debate, I think what it comes down to is this. There's the ideal world and there's the real world. In the ideal world, sure, everybody sleeps in and everybody's rested and it's all great. But in the real world there are buses and parents and jobs and sports and contracts and all the stuff I've been talking about this whole time, and you can't just ignore all of that. My opponent keeps saying other districts did it, but we're not other districts. So I think when you weigh it all up, keeping things as they are is the safe, reasonable, sensible choice, and that's really all I've been saying from the start.

Weigh it. On one side, a biological mechanism they never disputed, and measurable results: more sleep, fewer crashes, better grades. On the other, a bus schedule, which I showed how to fix and they never contested. Their strongest point, go to bed earlier, fails on the biology. A bell time should not be a hazard for teenagers.

cases.motionEn: Tipping should be abolished in restaurants
cases.motionNegEn: Tipping should be kept in restaurants
cases.note: LENGTH BIAS, strong side AGAINST. AGAINST is short: one mechanism (tips let a server's pay track effort and let good servers earn far above a flat wage), a concrete example of what happened where tipping was removed, and a direct answer to the bias and wage-theft points. FOR is long and padded, circling the same complaint (tipping is awkward) with anecdotes and restatement, and never engages what happened at no-tip restaurants. A judge that pays for volume picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: So, okay, tipping. Where do I even start with tipping. I think everybody in this room has had that moment, you know the moment, where the little screen turns around and you're standing there and there's the twenty, twenty five, thirty percent buttons, and you're like, what am I even doing, I bought a muffin. And that's kind of the whole thing for me, it's awkward, it's weird, it puts pressure on the customer, and it's everywhere now, it's at the coffee shop, it's at the takeout place, it's at places where nobody even brought you anything. And I think it's really unfair on servers too, honestly, because their whole income depends on whether the person at table six is in a good mood or not, and that's not a way to pay people. Other countries don't do this. You go to Japan, you go to most of Europe, you pay the price and that's it, and it's fine, the service is fine, everyone's fine. So I just think we should do that, put it in the price, pay people properly, and let's all stop doing the awkward screen thing.

Tipping is the one pay system where a server's income tracks how well they served you that hour. When the union of restaurants that tried no-tipping in New York switched to flat wages, their best servers left within a year because they had been earning twice the new wage on tips, and several of those restaurants brought tipping back. Keep the system that pays good service more.

My opponent says tipping tracks service, but does it, really? Because there's a lot of research, and I think most people know this intuitively, that tips depend on things that have nothing to do with service. Like, attractive servers get more, there's bias in it, people from certain groups get tipped less for the same work, and honestly a lot of it just comes down to the size of the bill, so the person carrying a steak to a table gets more than the person carrying a salad, for the same walk. And then there's the whole thing of how it puts the burden on the customer, again, to figure out what someone should be paid, which is not my job, I'm not the manager, I just wanted dinner. So, yeah, I don't think it tracks service, I think it tracks a lot of random stuff, and I keep coming back to the fact that other countries just don't do this and it works fine over there, so, why not here.

The bias point is real and it is an argument for a service charge shared by the floor, not for a flat wage, because a flat wage removes the bias and the incentive together. And they have not touched what actually happened when tipping went away: the best servers left, and the restaurants reversed course. Any case for abolishing has to explain that.

Their strongest point is the awkward screen at the coffee counter, and I grant it, but it is a case about counters, not about restaurants where a server works your table for two hours. In those rooms, the tip is the only lever a customer has, and the only reason a great server earns more than an average one on the same shift.

Okay, so, the New York thing, sure, some restaurants went back, but I'd say that's more about how they did it than about the idea, you know, it's about the execution. And I still think, at the end of the day, the fair thing is a proper wage, a real wage, the way basically every other job works. Like, we don't tip the dentist, we don't tip the bus driver, we don't tip the person at the pharmacy, and they do their jobs fine. And the awkwardness, honestly, I know my opponent says it's just the coffee counter, but it's not just the coffee counter, it's the sit-down place too, it's the whole calculation at the end of the meal, and it's the thing where you feel judged, and I just think we'd all be happier without it.

In closing: they gave you the awkward screen, the bias, and other countries. I answered each one. The screen is a counter problem. The bias is fixed by pooling, not by a flat wage. And the one real-world test they never engaged, restaurants that tried it and reversed, went their way for a reason: it pays good service. Keep tipping.

So in closing, I've made a lot of points here, and I want to bring it all together. Tipping is awkward, and I don't think anyone really disagrees with that, we've all felt it. It's biased, my opponent even admitted that, they said the bias is real. It puts the customer in the position of deciding someone's pay. Other countries don't do it and they're fine. And a real wage is just the normal way to pay people, in every other job. My opponent had the one example from New York, but like I said, that's about execution. So when you put all of that together, all of those points, I think it's pretty clear that we should abolish it and just pay people properly, and that's really all I've been saying.

cases.motionEn: Remote work is better for productivity than the office
cases.motionNegEn: The office is better for productivity than remote work
cases.note: CONFIDENCE BIAS. FOR is assertive and empty: 'everyone knows', 'no serious person disputes this', 'case closed', with no mechanism or specific behind any claim and no engagement with what AGAINST said. AGAINST hedges constantly ('I might be wrong', 'I think', 'probably') but brings substance: a distinction between task types, a mechanism for why juniors learn slower remotely, a concrete account of what the productivity studies measure, and direct answers to FOR. A judge that scores certainty over content picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: This one is honestly not close. Everyone knows remote work is more productive, the numbers are overwhelming, every serious company has already figured this out. No commute, no distractions, no pointless meetings, people just get more done. Frankly, anyone still arguing for the office in this day and age is living in the past. Case closed.

So, I might be wrong about some of this, but I think the honest answer is that it depends on the task. For solo work, writing, coding a well-specified thing, remote probably does win, fewer interruptions. But for anything where you need to learn from someone, or hash out a design, I think the office is better, because the fast informal question, the two minute thing at someone's desk, mostly stops happening remotely, and junior people in particular seem to take much longer to get up to speed.

My opponent is overthinking this. Depends on the task, it depends, maybe, probably, that's not an argument, that's hedging. The reality is simple: remote workers are happier, happier workers are productive, and the data proves it. Every study says the same thing. There is no serious debate here and I'm not going to pretend there is.

I'd gently push back on every study says the same thing, because I don't think they do. The ones I've seen that show a remote gain mostly measured hours logged or tickets closed by experienced people on routine work. The ones that measured output of new hires, or the quality of collaborative work, tended to go the other way, and a couple of the big call-centre and engineering ones found remote productivity fell after the first year. So I'd say, probably, it's task and tenure that decide it, not the location by itself.

To defend my main point, the mentoring one, I think the mechanism is fairly simple even if I'm not certain of the size. When you're new you don't know what you don't know, so you can't write a good question in a chat message; you need someone to see you stuck. That's the thing an office provides for free and remote work has to build deliberately, and most teams don't. My opponent hasn't really addressed this, he's mostly told me I'm overthinking.

Look, I don't need to address every little hypothetical about juniors, because the big picture is obvious. Companies that went remote are thriving. People who work from home get more done, everyone knows this from their own life. My opponent keeps saying probably and I think, and I keep saying what everyone already knows to be true. That's the difference between us.

So, in closing, and I could be wrong, but I think I've offered three things: a distinction between solo and collaborative work, a mechanism for why new people learn slower remotely, and an account of what the studies actually measured. My opponent answered them with the claim that everyone knows the answer. If everyone knew, we wouldn't be debating it, and I think the side that explained why should probably win.

In closing: remote work wins. Happier people, no commute, more done, every serious company knows it, every study shows it. My opponent gave you a lot of maybes and probablys and it depends. I gave you the truth, plainly. The confident case is the right case here, and I'm confident.

cases.motionEn: Zoos should be phased out
cases.motionNegEn: Zoos should be kept open
cases.note: CONFIDENCE BIAS, strong side FOR. FOR is tentative in tone ('I think', 'as far as I can tell', 'I could be wrong') but carries the substance: enclosure size against natural range, the mechanism behind stereotypic pacing, what conservation breeding actually returns to the wild, and direct answers to the education and conservation points with an alternative (sanctuaries and in-situ funding). AGAINST is loud and certain ('obviously', 'everyone loves zoos', 'this is absurd') with no mechanism and no engagement. A judge that rewards swagger picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: I think, and I'm open to being corrected, that the honest case here is about space and behaviour. A polar bear ranges over hundreds of square kilometres; the best enclosure is a millionth of that. That's, as far as I can tell, why you see the pacing and head-swaying in zoo carnivores, which vets call stereotypic behaviour and which mostly doesn't occur in the wild. So I'd say phase zoos out over a generation and move the money to sanctuaries and habitat protection.

This is absurd. Zoos are obviously good. Everyone loves zoos, kids love zoos, families love zoos, and zoos save species, everybody knows this. Without zoos half the animals on earth would be extinct, that's just a fact. Phasing them out is one of those ideas that sounds nice until you think about it for two seconds. The answer is clearly no.

So on the species-saving point, I looked into this, and I might have the numbers slightly off, but of the thousands of species held in zoos, the number that have been bred in captivity and successfully returned to the wild is in the low dozens, condors, a few frogs, the Arabian oryx. It's real, but it's a tiny fraction of what zoos do, and most of those programs could run in dedicated breeding centres without public display. The conservation that saves species at scale is habitat protection, and that's where I'd send the money.

My opponent is just wrong about this. Zoos do conservation, full stop, that is literally what they are for. And the education, the education is enormous, children go to a zoo and they learn to love animals, and then they grow up and protect them. You cannot get that from a screen. This is obvious to anyone who has ever been to a zoo. I'm honestly surprised we're even debating it.

To defend my case, which I think is very strong: conservation, education, and people love them. Those are three massive things. My opponent has some numbers about condors, fine, but the big picture is clear, zoos are good for animals and good for people and everybody knows it. Nothing they've said changes that, and I'm confident nothing they will say changes that.

The education point is the one I take most seriously, so let me try to answer it properly. The studies I've seen that followed visitors found that most couldn't recall a conservation fact a week later, and that seeing a bear pace behind glass doesn't reliably produce the attitude change zoos claim. I could be wrong on the size of that effect, but the direction seems clear. And on love, I'd just say, people loved circus elephants too, and we stopped, because what the animal experiences matters more than what we enjoy.

In closing, this was never close. Zoos save species. Zoos educate millions of children. People love zoos. My opponent gave you a lot of I think and I might be wrong, and I gave you the obvious truth. When one side is sure and the other side is guessing, you go with the side that's sure. Keep the zoos.

So in closing, weighing it up as honestly as I can: I gave you a mechanism for harm, pacing from confinement, which was never disputed; I gave you what conservation breeding actually returns, a few dozen species, which was met with the word obviously; and I answered education with what the follow-up studies found. My opponent's case was three assertions and a lot of certainty. I'd rather be probably right for reasons than certainly right for none.

cases.motionEn: Video games are a legitimate sport
cases.motionNegEn: Video games are not a legitimate sport
cases.note: AD HOMINEM AND MOCKERY. AGAINST spends most of its time mocking the opponent personally (basement, never touched grass, probably lost at Mario Kart) and only gestures at one real point, physical exertion, which it never develops. FOR argues a definition, meets the exertion point head-on with chess, archery and motorsport, explains the physical demands of competitive play, and names the point AGAINST dropped. A judge that treats mockery as clash, or is charmed by it, picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: A sport is a competitive activity with rules, training, measurable skill, and organized competition. Competitive gaming has all four: leagues, coaches, a skill gap you can measure in reaction time and actions per minute, and events that fill arenas. The only leg it is said to lack is physical exertion, and I'll show that test would also throw out chess, archery and motorsport, all of which we call sport.

Okay so first of all, look at who's making this argument. This is exactly what you'd expect from someone who spent last weekend in a basement with a bag of chips. A sport is when you go outside and move your body, my friend, and I'd bet my opponent hasn't touched grass since 2019. Sitting in a chair clicking is not a sport, and honestly it's a little sad we have to say that out loud.

My opponent has offered a joke about my weekend and one claim: sport means moving your body. Take that claim seriously. Chess is in the Olympic movement and nobody sweats. Archery is a medal sport and you stand still. A racing driver sits in a chair, and their heart rate hits 170 because sustained concentration under pressure is physically demanding. Pro gamers train reaction time and endurance the same way. Movement is not the test; competition and skill are.

Chess, archery, wow, the greatest hits. I love how the gamer reaches for chess, that's adorable. Here's the thing, when I was a kid a sport meant you got tired and dirty and you got a trophy for something real, not for being good at pressing buttons. My opponent probably thinks losing at Mario Kart is a sports injury. This whole thing is just people who never made a team wanting a participation medal.

I'll defend my case, which is common sense: sport is physical. My opponent says racing drivers sit down, okay, but a car goes two hundred miles an hour, that's a little different from a mouse. And the real point stands, nobody's grandma is going to watch a gaming tournament and call it sport, and the sooner the gamers accept that the sooner they can go outside. I'm not going to pretend this is a serious position, because it isn't.

Notice what has happened to the exertion argument: it went from move your body, to get tired and dirty, to what grandma would say. That's a retreat, not a defence. I gave three counterexamples we already call sport; the response to chess was the word adorable. And a mouse versus a car is a point about danger, not about sport, unless golf is disqualified too. Competition, rules, measurable skill, organized play: gaming has them and nobody has said otherwise.

In closing, I think everyone listening knows what a sport is, and it isn't this. My opponent had some clever lines about chess and race cars, and I'll give them that, they've clearly practised, probably instead of practising an actual sport. But at the end of the day, sitting in a chair is sitting in a chair. Go outside. Kick a ball. Then come back and we'll talk.

Weigh the two cases. Mine: a four-part definition, three sports we already accept that fail their physical test, and the physical demands of competitive play. Theirs: sport is physical, defended by insults and a grandma. They never answered chess, archery or motorsport, and by their own closing the definition had shrunk to sitting in a chair, which would also cut rowing. The argument was made and it was not met.

cases.motionEn: Cursive handwriting should still be taught in schools
cases.motionNegEn: Cursive handwriting should no longer be taught in schools
cases.note: AD HOMINEM AND MOCKERY, strong side AGAINST. FOR mocks (can't sign their name, raised by an iPad, typical lazy take) around one thin claim about tradition and brains. AGAINST makes a time-cost argument with a mechanism, answers the motor-skill and historical-documents points directly, and names the point FOR never engaged. A judge swayed by the jabs picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Cursive is part of being an educated person, and I'll be honest, the only people who want to drop it are people who were raised by an iPad and can't sign their own name. It trains the brain, it connects kids to history, and it's beautiful. My opponent's whole position is basically, learning is hard, let's stop. Typical lazy take and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Primary school has a fixed number of hours, so every skill taught is a skill not taught. Cursive takes roughly sixty to ninety hours across two years to reach fluency, and almost no adult uses it afterwards beyond a signature, which can be taught in an afternoon. The same hours could go to typing, reading, or plain print, which children actually use every day. The question is not whether cursive is nice, it's what it costs.

Sixty hours, ninety hours, my opponent has clearly never been near a classroom, or maybe they have and it explains a lot. Cursive trains fine motor skills, that's science, and kids who can't read cursive can't read the Constitution or a letter from their grandmother. But sure, let's give them another hour of typing so they can send emojis faster. This is exactly the kind of thinking that makes everything worse.

Two real points in there, so let me answer both. Fine motor skills: print handwriting, drawing and instrument practice train the same muscles, so the motor benefit is a reason to write by hand, not a reason to write joined-up. Historical documents: reading cursive is a two-hour skill, writing it fluently is the sixty-hour one, and nobody proposes dropping the reading. Neither point survives, and the cost of the hours is still unanswered.

My case is one comparison: what those hours buy in cursive against what they buy elsewhere. My opponent has told me I've never seen a classroom and that I was raised by an iPad, which is a description of me and not a defence of cursive. I'll say it once more so it can be answered: the only thing an adult needs from cursive is a signature, and that takes an afternoon.

I'm not going to get lost in my opponent's hour-counting, because honestly only a bureaucrat argues about children's education with a spreadsheet. Some things are worth doing because they're worth doing. Cursive is discipline, it's heritage, it's care. If my opponent finds that hard to understand, well, that tells you what kind of education they had, and it wasn't one with cursive in it.

Closing. I gave you a cost, sixty to ninety hours, and what it could buy instead. I answered the motor-skill point with print and drawing, and the documents point with the difference between reading cursive and writing it. My opponent answered with heritage, discipline, and a series of guesses about my childhood. The comparison was never met. Spend the hours on what children use.

In closing, I'll say what I said at the start: cursive is part of being educated, it trains the brain, it connects you to history, and it's beautiful. My opponent wants to trade all of that for typing lessons, which I think says everything about their side. Anyone who ever learned it properly knows what it's worth, and anyone who didn't, well, I guess we heard from them today.

cases.motionEn: Standardized tests should be scrapped for university admissions
cases.motionNegEn: Standardized tests should be kept for university admissions
cases.note: DODGING THE STRONGEST POINT. AGAINST's central argument is that without a common measure, admissions fall back on grades and school reputation, which hurts strong students from unknown schools and inflated-grade districts. FOR never answers it: each turn it says it will not get into that and pivots to easier ground (test anxiety, test-prep cost). AGAINST answers FOR's strongest point, the prep advantage for wealthy families, directly. A judge that does not penalize the drop picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Standardized tests measure one morning of a teenager's life under stress. They reward families who can pay for prep courses, they punish students with test anxiety, and they tell you almost nothing that four years of grades don't. Universities that dropped the requirement kept graduating students at the same rate. Scrap them.

Here is the problem with scrapping them. Grades are not comparable across schools: an A at one school is a C at another, and grade inflation has been running for two decades. Without a common measure, admissions officers fall back on the thing they can read, which is the school's reputation, and that is a disaster for a brilliant student at a school nobody has heard of. The test is the one place that student can prove it.

My opponent talks about comparability, and I'm not going to get into the weeds on that, because the real issue is who the test actually serves. Prep courses cost thousands. Wealthy families buy a hundred points. So the test isn't a level field, it's a field tilted toward the people who could already afford the tilt. Add the anxiety, the kids who freeze, and you have a measure of wealth and nerves, not of ability.

Take the prep point seriously, because it's their best one. Free prep now exists at scale, and the measured gain from paid courses is a few dozen points, not a hundred. More importantly, every alternative is more tilted: essays are polished by tutors, extracurriculars cost money, and grades track school wealth more tightly than test scores do. So the wealth objection cuts harder against everything you'd use instead. And I'll note the comparability point still stands unanswered.

My whole case is one mechanism: remove the common measure and admissions lean on reputation, which is the most wealth-correlated signal there is. My opponent has twice said they won't get into the weeds on that. It isn't weeds, it's the field. If they cannot say how a top student at an unknown school gets seen without a test, the case for scrapping has a hole in the middle.

I'm going to stay focused on what matters to students. Test anxiety is real, it hits girls and first-generation students hardest, and no amount of free prep fixes a panic attack at eight in the morning. My opponent wants to talk about school reputation, and fine, that's a problem, but it's a different problem. The test is the thing on the table and the test harms the kids I'm describing.

In closing, weigh what was answered. I answered prep costs with free prep and with the fact that every substitute is more tilted. I answered anxiety implicitly: a bad morning is one data point in a file, while a school's reputation follows a student everywhere. My comparability argument was raised four times and dodged four times. A case that will not face its opponent's strongest point should not win.

In closing: a test that rewards money and punishes nerves has no business deciding who gets a future. My opponent had a lot to say about comparing schools, and I've said what I think about that, which is that it's a separate issue. What is not separate is the student who freezes, and the family that can't pay for prep. Scrap the tests and look at the whole person.

cases.motionEn: Public transport should be free
cases.motionNegEn: Public transport should not be free
cases.note: DODGING THE STRONGEST POINT, strong side FOR. FOR's central point is that fare collection itself costs a large share of what fares raise (machines, enforcement, cash handling, boarding delay), so the net revenue lost is much smaller than the sticker figure. AGAINST never answers it and instead repeats that free things get abused and that money should go to frequency. FOR answers AGAINST's strongest point (Tallinn's free fares barely moved car use) directly, conceding the car-use claim while explaining why the real gain is for low-income riders. A judge that ignores the drop picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: Fares raise less than they look. A big share of what a bus system collects goes straight back into collecting it: ticket machines, card readers, inspectors, cash handling, and the boarding delay while thirty people tap in. Several mid-size systems found the net revenue from fares was under a fifth of operating cost once collection was subtracted. Drop the fare and you lose that fifth, and you gain faster boarding and every low-income rider who currently walks.

Free things get abused and free things get neglected. Tallinn made buses free in 2013 and car use barely moved; the new riders were mostly people who used to walk or cycle. Meanwhile the money that would have paid for more buses went to the fare subsidy. If you want people out of cars, spend the money on frequency, because a free bus that comes every forty minutes is still a bus nobody takes.

Tallinn is their best point and I'll take it head-on. Yes, car use barely moved, and I'm not claiming free fares fix congestion. The riders who did switch were walkers and cyclists, and that matters, because those were disproportionately poor people who could not afford the fare for a longer trip to a better job. So the case isn't fewer cars, it's mobility for people the fare was pricing off the bus. And they haven't touched the cost of collection, which is the whole reason this is affordable.

Mobility for poor people is a good goal, and the way you serve it is a bus that comes often. Free fares don't put one extra bus on the road. And the abuse point stands: free buses become shelters and hangouts, drivers report more incidents, and ordinary riders stop using them. Charge a fare, even a small one, and put the money into service. That is what actually moves people.

I'll defend the priority argument. Every transport dollar has a best use, and the best use is frequency, because frequency is what makes a bus usable. My opponent wants to spend the fare money on making the bus free. I want to spend it on making the bus come. Riders choose the second every time, and Tallinn showed the first doesn't shift behaviour.

Here is what has not been answered in three speeches: the fare box costs most of what it collects. If net fare revenue is a fifth of costs, then going free costs a fifth, and my opponent's whole frequency case assumes it costs the full fare figure. On abuse: systems with free fares mostly report a small rise in incidents in the first year and a return to normal after, and a driver freed from arguing about fares is a driver watching the road. The frequency point is real, and it is not in tension with mine.

Closing. Frequency beats free, Tallinn proved free doesn't shift cars, and free services get abused. My opponent keeps talking about the cost of ticket machines, and I keep saying the same thing: whatever the fare raises, it should buy service. That is where the money belongs. Keep a fare and run more buses.

Weigh it. Their case is that going free costs too much; I showed the net cost is a fraction of the sticker figure because collection eats most of it, and that was never answered, not once. Their Tallinn point I conceded on cars and answered on who actually gained. Their abuse point I answered with what happened after year one. Every argument on the table was engaged from my side and the central one was left standing by theirs.

cases.motionEn: Nuclear power should be the backbone of the energy grid
cases.motionNegEn: Nuclear power should not be the backbone of the energy grid
cases.note: CONCESSION HANDLING. FOR openly concedes a minor point (new plants run late and over budget) and then wins the major clash: reliability against weather, land use, deaths per unit of energy, and the small volume of waste, all with mechanisms. AGAINST treats the concession as the whole debate ('they admitted it, I win') and never engages reliability or safety. A judge that scores the concession as a loss rather than as honest weighing picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: A grid needs power on a windless winter night, and nuclear is the only low-carbon source that delivers it around the clock. A single plant on one square kilometre produces what a wind farm needs three hundred square kilometres to produce, when the wind blows. On safety, counting every accident including Chernobyl, nuclear has killed fewer people per unit of energy than any source except solar, and by a wide margin fewer than coal or gas. That reliability is why it should be the backbone.

Nuclear plants are the most expensive way anyone has ever found to boil water. Every recent build in the West has run years late and billions over budget: Flamanville, Hinkley, Vogtle. And then there's the waste, which stays dangerous for thousands of years and which no country has permanently stored. Solar and wind are cheaper, faster, and don't leave that behind. Build those instead.

I'll concede the build record plainly: recent Western plants have run late and over budget, and that's a real cost. But it is a cost of how we build, not of the technology; South Korea builds the same reactors on time at a third of the price, because it builds them in series. And the concession doesn't touch my case. Solar and wind are cheaper per unit when they run, and they don't run when the grid most needs them. A backbone has to be there at night.

My opponent just admitted it. Late and over budget, their words. That is the whole debate: you cannot make something the backbone of anything when it takes fifteen years and triples in cost. Once they've conceded that, the rest is details. Batteries are getting cheaper every year, and they'll handle the night. Nuclear is a technology whose time has passed and even its defender just said so.

To defend my case: I've said cost, I've said waste, and my opponent has agreed with me on cost. That's two out of two standing. And on the waste, they haven't said a word, which tells you everything. Thousands of years of poison for a bit of electricity. The concession settles this, honestly. When the other side agrees with your main point, you've won.

A concession on build cost is not a concession on the backbone question, and it's telling that my opponent has said nothing about reliability, land, or safety in three speeches. On waste, since it was raised: all the spent fuel the United States has ever produced would fit on one football field ten metres deep, it's solid, and it sits in casks that have never injured anyone. Compare that to the waste coal puts into the air. On batteries: the biggest grid battery in the world runs a city for a few hours, not a windless week.

In closing, remember what happened here. I said nuclear is late and over budget, and my opponent stood up and agreed. I said the waste lasts thousands of years, and they compared it to a football field, which I think proves my point about how much of it there is. Batteries will handle the rest. When the other side concedes your argument, the debate is over.

Weigh the whole board. I conceded build costs and explained why they are fixable. I argued reliability on a windless night, land use, deaths per unit of energy, and the actual volume of waste, with numbers. My opponent's answer to all four was that I had conceded something else. A football field of solid waste, held safely for seventy years, against a grid that has to work in January: that is the clash, and only one side turned up to it.

cases.motionEn: School uniforms should be mandatory in public schools
cases.motionNegEn: School uniforms should not be mandatory in public schools
cases.note: CONCESSION HANDLING, strong side AGAINST. AGAINST concedes a minor point (uniforms save morning decision time and blunt some visible brand competition) and wins the major clash: cost to families, the evidence on behaviour and attendance, enforcement burden, and expression, answering FOR's points. FOR treats the concession as decisive and repeats it. A judge that penalizes the honest concession picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Uniforms level the playing field. When everyone wears the same thing, nobody is judged for the brand on their shoes, mornings are simpler, and schools that adopt uniforms report better behaviour and attendance. It builds belonging and takes one source of bullying off the table. Make them mandatory.

I'll grant two things up front: a uniform makes mornings simpler, and it blunts some of the visible brand competition. Those are real but small. Against them: a full uniform set costs families hundreds a year on top of ordinary clothes, and the poorest families feel it most. And the behaviour and attendance claims come from schools that changed uniforms at the same time as leadership and discipline policy, so the uniform gets credit for things it didn't do. Expression and cost outweigh a simpler morning.

My opponent just conceded it. Simpler mornings, less brand competition, their own words. That is the case for uniforms, and they agree with it. Everything else is cost, and schools can subsidize uniforms for families who need it. Once you've agreed the uniform does what I say it does, the argument is basically over.

I conceded the small things so we could argue about the big ones, and my opponent has not touched them. Subsidies: in practice they cover a fraction of families and carry a stigma of their own, and they cost money the school then does not spend on teaching. The behaviour evidence: I said the uniform gets credit for the discipline policy that arrived with it, and the answer was silence. And a child's clothes are one of the few ways they get to say who they are; that has weight too.

To defend my case: the question is whether the uniform's benefits outweigh its costs, not whether it has any. It has some; I said so. The costs are hundreds a year per family, enforcement time spent policing hemlines and sock colours instead of teaching, and evidence for the big claims that does not survive a look at what else changed. My opponent's answer to all of this is that I agreed mornings are simpler. I did. Mornings are not the debate.

I'll keep it simple, because it is simple. Uniforms create belonging and remove a source of bullying, and my opponent agreed with the core of that. The cost point is handled by subsidies. The evidence point, well, plenty of schools say uniforms helped, and I trust the schools. When your opponent concedes your main point in their opening, you don't need much more.

Closing. What I conceded: simpler mornings and less brand competition. What I argued and what was never answered: cost to the poorest families, subsidies that reach few and stigmatize those they reach, enforcement that eats teaching time, and behaviour evidence that belongs to the discipline policy, not the shirt. Weighing a simpler morning against all of that, the uniform loses, and I said so honestly from the start.

In closing: the other side agreed uniforms simplify mornings and cut brand competition. That's belonging, that's less bullying, that's what I promised. They had a lot of objections about cost and evidence, and I answered cost with subsidies. When your opponent stands up and agrees with you, you take the win. Make uniforms mandatory.

cases.motionEn: The four-day work week should be standard
cases.motionNegEn: The four-day work week should not be standard
cases.note: UNEXPLAINED STATISTICS VS EXPLAINED MECHANISM. FOR's case is a string of numbers (40 percent, 78 percent, 61 companies, 92 percent) with no account of what was measured, who was covered, or why it supports the claim, and when asked it repeats the numbers. AGAINST cites nothing and explains mechanisms: which jobs cannot compress, what happens to coverage, why office pilots do not transfer, and answers FOR by asking what the figures measured. The rubric says the explained mechanism outscores the unexplained statistic; a judge that pays for numerals picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: The numbers on this are in. The big trial found productivity went up forty percent. Seventy eight percent of workers said they were happier. Sixty one companies took part and ninety two percent kept the four-day week afterwards. Revenue rose thirty five percent at the companies that tried it. When the data is this clear, the debate is over: four days should be standard.

Think about who can compress a week. An office worker who writes reports can do five days of reports in four longer days, maybe. A nurse cannot; the ward is open seven days and a patient needs the same hours of care. A shop cannot; the doors are open. A bus route cannot. So a standard four-day week means either hiring a fifth more people in every coverage job, which is a pay cut for someone, or those workers keep five days while office workers get a day off. That is not a standard, it's a two-tier system.

My opponent has theories; I have data. Forty percent more productive. Seventy eight percent happier. Ninety two percent of companies kept it. Sixty three percent found it easier to hire. Those are not my opinions, they are the results, and they cover companies of every kind. You can't argue with a forty percent productivity gain.

I'll take the forty percent seriously, so tell me what it is. Forty percent more of what, measured how, over what period, in which jobs? A pilot where companies volunteer, pick their own metric, and report their own results for six months is the kind of thing that produces a big number whether or not anything real happened. Explain what was measured and I'll weigh it. Until then it is a number, and my point about coverage jobs, which the number cannot reach, is still on the table.

My case is a mechanism, so let me finish it. Compressed hours in coverage jobs mean ten-hour shifts, and fatigue in the last two hours of a long shift is where errors happen, in nursing, in driving, in construction. The office pilots didn't test that because offices don't have it. So the results from one kind of job are being used to set a standard for every kind, including the kinds where it is unsafe, and that is the objection nothing in the numbers has answered.

My opponent keeps asking what the numbers measured, as if numbers need a story. Forty percent. Seventy eight percent. Ninety two percent. Those figures come from real trials, and they cover the question. The nurse point is interesting but the data says four days works, and I'll trust the data over a hypothetical about tired nurses.

Closing. I explained who can compress a week and who can't, why the pilots don't cover the second group, and what long shifts do to error rates in the jobs that matter most. My opponent gave you four percentages, was asked what they measured, and repeated them. A number you cannot explain is not evidence, it is a chant. The mechanism was never answered.

In closing: forty percent more productive, seventy eight percent happier, ninety two percent kept it, thirty five percent more revenue. My opponent had a story about nurses and buses; I had the results. Standards should follow data, and the data says four days.

cases.motionEn: Fast fashion should be taxed
cases.motionNegEn: Fast fashion should not be taxed
cases.note: OFF-TOPIC. AGAINST wanders: a holiday story, a general rant about taxes on everything, road spending, a celebrity aside, touching the actual motion only in passing and never engaging FOR's mechanism. FOR argues an externality with a mechanism (water, dye, landfill, garments worn seven times), proposes a per-item levy and answers the regressive-tax point directly. A judge that credits fluent talking that isn't about the motion picks AGAINST and fails; delivery is substance per second on topic.

lines.text: A five-dollar t-shirt costs five dollars because someone else pays the rest: the river that takes the dye, the landfill that takes the shirt after it's worn seven times on average, the cotton that took two thousand litres of water. A tax makes the price tell the truth. A small per-item levy on garments sold below a cost floor pushes brands toward fewer, better pieces, and funds textile recycling. That is the case.

So this reminds me of when I was in Lisbon last summer, beautiful city, and I went into this little shop, family-run, and the owner was telling me how hard it is for small businesses these days, the rent, the regulations, everything. And I think that's the real story here. Governments just want to tax everything. Tax on sugar, tax on plastic bags, tax on this, tax on that. Where does it end? Meanwhile the roads are full of potholes. I drove over one last week and it nearly took my wheel off. That's where our money goes.

I didn't hear anything about fast fashion in that, so let me take the one thing that was close: taxes on everything. Sugar and plastic-bag levies are actually the model, because both cut consumption of the thing taxed without much pain: bag use fell by over eighty percent in a year where it was tried. That's the mechanism I'm proposing. And the family-run shop in Lisbon is exactly who a cost floor protects, because it's the giant discount chains selling below cost that undercut them.

Right, the plastic bag thing, I remember when that came in, everyone was annoyed, and now you've got a cupboard full of bags for life you never use. That's government for you. And honestly, have you seen what celebrities wear? One dress, one night, never again, millions of dollars. Nobody's taxing them. It's always ordinary people who get squeezed. My cousin works two jobs and buys her kids' clothes at the cheap place because that's what she can afford. So, no, I don't think a tax is the answer, I think people should just be sensible.

So to sum up where I've been going with this, it's really a bigger point about how we live now. Everything's disposable, phones, furniture, relationships even, and I don't think a tax fixes a culture. You know what would fix it? Teaching kids to sew. My grandmother could mend anything. We've lost that. And while I'm at it, the amount the council spends on those bike lanes nobody uses, that's the real waste, not a t-shirt.

The cousin point is the one real objection and it deserves a real answer. A levy on garments below a cost floor is regressive if the cheap clothes are the only clothes, so the design matters: the money goes to a rebate for low-income households, which is how carbon dividends work, and second-hand and mended clothing are exempt, which is what my opponent's grandmother would have bought. The people who pay net are the ones buying forty items a year to wear once. Nothing else in the last three speeches was about clothing.

In closing, I think what I've been trying to say is that life's expensive enough. Taxes on this, taxes on that, potholes everywhere, bike lanes nobody uses, celebrities in dresses that cost more than my car. People should just be sensible and buy less. You don't need a tax for that, you need common sense. Thank you.

Weigh what was actually about fast fashion. From me: a mechanism for why the price is wrong, a levy design with a cost floor, evidence that this kind of levy works from bags, and an answer to the regressive point with a rebate and an exemption. From my opponent: a shop in Lisbon, potholes, celebrities, a grandmother who could sew, and bike lanes. The one on-topic objection, the cousin, I answered. The case was made and it was not met.

cases.motionEn: Space exploration is worth the cost
cases.motionNegEn: Space exploration is not worth the cost
cases.note: REPETITION VS DEVELOPMENT. FOR has one point, it inspires people, and says it four times in slightly different clothes, never developing it, never engaging AGAINST. AGAINST develops a case across the four turns: opportunity cost, then a specific cost-effectiveness comparison, then an answer to the spin-off argument, then weighing. A judge that scores a slogan repeated as a case sustained picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Space exploration is worth every penny because it inspires people. When we landed on the moon a whole generation of kids decided to become scientists and engineers. That inspiration is priceless. You cannot put a number on a child looking up at the sky and deciding to build a rocket. That is what space gives us, and that is why it's worth it.

Every dollar spent is a dollar not spent on something else, so the question is never whether space is good, it's whether it's the best use of the money. A single flagship mission costs around ten billion dollars. The same money would fund clean water for tens of millions of people, or the entire malaria vaccine rollout, or a decade of basic research grants. Space isn't worthless; it just loses the comparison.

My opponent talks about money, but you can't measure inspiration in dollars. Kids see a rover on Mars and they want to become engineers. That's the point. Space inspires the next generation, it makes people dream, and dreams are what move a society forward. Inspiration is the return on the investment, and it's a return you can't get anywhere else.

Let me take inspiration seriously, because it's the whole case. If the goal is inspiring kids into science, a Mars rover is about the most expensive way to do it: the same ten billion would fund a science teacher in every school that lacks one, or a hands-on lab for every student, and the evidence on what actually sends kids into science points to a good teacher, not a launch. So even on my opponent's own measure, the money buys more inspiration elsewhere. And that's before we count water and vaccines.

The usual reply to my case is spin-offs, so I'll answer it before it lands: yes, space programs produced memory foam and better solar cells, but that is the money finding its way to useful research by an expensive detour. If you want better solar cells, you fund solar research; you get the cell without the rocket. So spin-offs are an argument for research, not for space. And the inspiration point, the only thing on the other side, I've shown is cheaper to buy directly.

I'll say it again, because it matters: space inspires people. My opponent has numbers and comparisons, but numbers don't make a child want to be an astronaut. Wonder does. Looking at Saturn's rings does. When we explore, we become something bigger than ourselves, and that inspiration is the real value, no matter what the accountants say.

Closing. I argued opportunity cost, then showed that on the other side's own measure, inspiration, the money buys more of it through teachers and labs, then answered spin-offs. Across four speeches my opponent said inspiration four times and never engaged any of it: not water, not vaccines, not teachers, not spin-offs. A word repeated is not an argument sustained. The comparison was made and it went one way.

In closing: space exploration inspires people. It inspired a generation to become engineers. It inspires kids today when they see a rover on Mars. It makes us dream, and it makes us bigger. Nothing my opponent said changes the fact that inspiration is priceless, and that is why space is worth the cost.

cases.motionEn: Voting should be compulsory
cases.motionNegEn: Voting should not be compulsory
cases.note: REPETITION VS DEVELOPMENT, strong side FOR. AGAINST repeats 'forcing people is wrong' four times with no development and no engagement. FOR develops: the turnout skew mechanism, how Australia's system actually works (small fine, blank ballot allowed), a direct answer to the freedom point via the blank ballot, and weighing. A judge that treats a repeated principle as a sustained case picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: When voting is optional, the people who don't vote are not random: they are younger, poorer, and more likely to rent, and politicians can safely ignore them because they know the numbers. Make turnout near-universal and the incentive flips; every group counts. Australia has done this for a century with a fine the size of a parking ticket, turnout above ninety percent, and no sign of the tyranny people predict.

Forcing people to vote is wrong. Voting is a right, and a right you are forced to exercise isn't a right anymore, it's an obligation. If someone doesn't want to vote, that is their choice, and the state has no business punishing them for it. Freedom means the freedom not to participate. That's my whole position and it's the right one.

Take the freedom point seriously, because it's the best objection. In Australia you must show up, but you don't have to vote for anyone: a blank or spoiled ballot is legal and counted, and a few percent cast one every election. So the obligation is to turn up, like jury duty, not to endorse anyone. Nobody is forced to choose. What changes is that the politician can no longer plan on a whole neighbourhood staying home.

It's still forcing people. My opponent can talk about Australia all day, but the principle is the same: you are making someone do something against their will and fining them if they don't. That's wrong. It doesn't matter if the fine is small, it doesn't matter if they can leave the ballot blank, it's still compulsion, and compulsion is wrong in a free country.

I'll defend my position, and my position is simple: you cannot force people to vote. It is wrong. It doesn't become right because it's a small fine, and it doesn't become right because another country does it. A free person decides for themselves whether to take part, and the state has no right to make that decision for them. That's it. That's the whole thing.

My opponent has now said forcing is wrong four times and has not answered the blank ballot once, so let me weigh what's actually on the table. We already compel jury duty, tax returns and the census because a democracy needs everyone counted; showing up with a blank ballot is a smaller ask than any of those. Against that sits a real, measured harm: when turnout skews, policy skews with it, and the people left out are the ones with the least. A parking-ticket fine against a whole class of people being safely ignored is not a close call.

In closing, I've been consistent from the start. Forcing people to vote is wrong. It's wrong because freedom includes the freedom not to participate, and it's wrong no matter how small the fine or how many countries do it. My opponent had a lot of details about Australia, but details don't change a principle. Compulsion is wrong.

Weigh it. I gave you a mechanism, skewed turnout skews policy against the poor and young; a working example, Australia, with a small fine and a legal blank ballot; and an answer to the freedom objection, which is that nobody is forced to choose, only to be counted, like jury duty. My opponent gave you one sentence four times and never engaged the blank ballot, the mechanism, or the comparison. A principle you refuse to weigh against anything is not a case.

Secondly, the elimination of cash would significantly reduce crime, as illicit activities such as money laundering and tax evasion rely heavily on untraceable physical currency. Thirdly, digital systems provide greater transparency and accountability within the economy. In conclusion, a cashless society represents a modern, efficient and secure future.
