And the fee, two to three percent on every single purchase in the country, that's a tax that goes to Visa, and nobody voted for it.

um, so, defending my case, the strongest thing I've got is the power cut, because it's not a hypothetical, it happened, and every cashless system has a version of it, the outage, the bank IT failure, the app that's down, and in that moment cash is the only thing that works. And nobody's answered it. The nan point, they said financial inclusion initiatives, which, I don't know what that means for an eighty four year old who doesn't have a smartphone. And the fee is still there, every purchase, forever.

In addressing the concerns raised, it is essential to recognise that no system is without its challenges. Nevertheless, the advantages of a cashless society are clear and well documented. Enhanced security, reduced transaction costs for businesses, improved tax compliance and greater convenience for consumers all contribute to a stronger economy. Additionally, governments and financial institutions are well positioned to support vulnerable populations through the transition. On balance, the case for phasing out cash remains robust.

ok closing, um, I said three things at the start, the outage, the old lady, the fee, and I said them again, and I'm still waiting on an answer to any of them, like the reply was no system is without challenges, which, yeah. And they said reduced transaction costs for businesses which is just wrong, the card fee is a transaction cost, it's the whole reason the coffee costs fifty cents more. So I've got three real things nobody touched, and they've got a paragraph that could've been about any topic. Keep cash.

In conclusion, the case for phasing out cash rests on convenience, security and transparency. While the opposing side has raised anecdotal concerns, these do not outweigh the systemic benefits of a modern digital economy. It is important to note that progress inevitably involves adaptation, and society has successfully navigated similar transitions before. For these reasons, cash should be phased out.

cases.motionEn: Children under fourteen should not have smartphones
cases.motionNegEn: Children under fourteen should be allowed smartphones
cases.note: CHATBOT PASTE, strong side FOR. AGAINST is polished generic essay text (It is important to note, Furthermore, a balanced approach, In conclusion) that never responds to the specific points FOR raises and answers 'critics' rather than the opponent. FOR is a scrappy speaker with fillers who brings specifics (the group chat at 2am, the flip phone compromise, what the school saw when it locked phones away) and answers AGAINST's safety and digital-literacy points directly. A judge that rewards the tidy paragraph over engagement picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: so, ok, my thing is basically this. My little brother got a phone at eleven and within a month he was in a group chat that went till two in the morning, every night, and his grades fell off a cliff and he got mean, like properly mean, and when we took it away he was back to himself in about three weeks. I'm not saying no phone, a flip phone for calls is fine, that's the compromise, but the smartphone, the apps, the feed, not before fourteen. The school that locked them in pouches said fights went down and kids started talking at lunch again.

Smartphones are an integral part of modern life, and children should not be excluded from them. Firstly, smartphones provide essential safety benefits, allowing parents to stay in contact with their children at all times. Secondly, they are a valuable educational tool, offering access to a wealth of information and learning resources. Thirdly, digital literacy is a critical skill in the twenty-first century, and early exposure helps children develop it. In conclusion, a balanced approach that includes parental guidance is preferable to an outright ban.

right so safety, ok, a flip phone does that, calls and texts, that's the whole point of the compromise I said, you don't need TikTok to ring your mum. Educational tool, um, I've watched my brother use it, it's not for learning, and every study I've seen on phones in classrooms says grades go down, not up. And digital literacy, like, learning to use an app is not hard, kids pick it up in a day at fourteen, you don't need three years of practice for that, the thing that takes three years to recover from is the group chat at two am.

While critics may argue that smartphones are a distraction, it is important to note that technology itself is neutral, and its impact depends on how it is used. Furthermore, banning smartphones fails to address the underlying issues and may leave children unprepared for the digital world. Moreover, responsible use can be taught through parental controls and open communication. Ultimately, education and guidance are more effective than prohibition.

In defending my position, it is essential to emphasise that smartphones offer significant benefits when used appropriately. Parental controls, screen time limits and age-appropriate content filters provide effective safeguards. Additionally, excluding children from technology may create social isolation, as their peers will have access to it. A balanced, guided approach remains the most reasonable path forward.

ok so, um, they said parental controls, and like, my parents had controls on, my brother had the group chat on a second account in ten minutes, every kid knows how, so that's not an answer, that's a hope. And social isolation, that's actually the best point they've got, so, the school with the pouches, when nobody has one at lunch nobody's isolated, that's the whole reason it has to be an age rule and not just my family's rule. And I notice they've said technology is neutral and balanced approach twice and haven't said anything about my actual brother or the school.

In conclusion, smartphones provide safety, education and digital literacy, and these benefits outweigh the potential drawbacks. While the opposing side has shared personal anecdotes, a comprehensive approach based on parental guidance and responsible use is more effective than an arbitrary age limit. It is important to note that preparing children for the digital world is a responsibility we cannot ignore. For these reasons, children should be allowed smartphones.

closing, um, weigh it. I gave you what happened to one kid, what happened at one school, and a compromise, the flip phone, that answers safety completely. I answered education with what the classroom studies show, digital literacy with how fast kids pick it up, controls with how fast they get round them, and isolation with the pouch school. They gave you three headings and the word balanced, and they never once talked about the group chat, the school, or the flip phone. One side was in this debate and the other side was reading.

cases.motionEn: Single-use plastic bags should be banned in supermarkets
cases.motionNegEn: Single-use plastic bags should not be banned in supermarkets
cases.note: UNEXPLAINED STATISTICS VS EXPLAINED MECHANISM, strong side FOR. AGAINST is a string of unexplained figures (0.6 percent of litter, 131 uses, 340 percent, 7,000 jobs) with no account of what was measured or why it supports the claim, and when asked it repeats them. FOR cites no numbers beyond what it explains: the default-changing mechanism, why a bag used for minutes persists for centuries, what happened at checkouts where a charge was introduced and why, and a direct answer to the cotton-bag and jobs points. The rubric says the explained mechanism outscores the unexplained statistic; a judge that pays for numerals picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: The case is about defaults. At a checkout the bag is free, it appears without asking, and so people take four when they need one, because the cost of taking one is zero and the cost of refusing is a small awkward moment. Change the default, either by charging or by removing them, and the same shopper brings a bag from the car, because now the awkward moment costs money. That is why every place that charged even a few cents saw bag use collapse within months: not because people were persuaded, but because the default flipped. And a bag that does twenty minutes of work then spends centuries in a hedge or a river is a bad trade for twenty minutes.

The data does not support a ban. Plastic bags are only zero point six percent of litter. A cotton bag has to be used one hundred and thirty one times to break even. After the ban in one state, sales of bin liners rose three hundred and forty percent. Seven thousand jobs depend on bag manufacturing. Paper bags produce seventy percent more emissions. Those are the numbers, and the numbers say a ban does more harm than good.

Take the cotton bag figure, since it is the one that sounds strongest. The comparison assumes the alternative is a heavy cotton tote made new for the purpose. The actual alternative at most checkouts is the bag you already own, a rucksack, or a thick reusable plastic bag that costs a few cents and does hundreds of trips, which is what shoppers switched to in practice. And on bin liners: yes, some people were reusing free bags as bin liners, and after a ban they buy liners instead, so a part of the drop is displaced. But a bought liner is one bag used once for its purpose, not four taken by reflex and one used, which is the waste a ban removes.

My opponent has theories about defaults; I have the numbers. Zero point six percent of litter. One hundred and thirty one uses. Three hundred and forty percent more bin liner sales. Seven thousand jobs. Seventy percent more emissions from paper. You cannot argue with a three hundred and forty percent increase. These are published findings and they cover the question.

To defend my case: the evidence is on my side and my opponent has not produced a single figure. I have five. Litter, break-even uses, bin liners, jobs, paper emissions. When one side has data and the other side has a story about awkward moments at the till, you go with the data. The ban sounds green and the numbers say it is not.

A number is only as good as what it measures, so let me ask what these measure. Zero point six percent of litter, by what, by count or by weight, and of what, street litter or the stuff in rivers, because a bag weighs almost nothing and so a weight share tells you nothing about how many there are. Three hundred and forty percent of what starting figure, in what time window. No answer has come in three speeches. Meanwhile the mechanism I described, flip the default and use collapses, is something anyone here has seen at a till in the last five years. On jobs: the same factories make the thick reusable bags, and a job making a product that ends up in a hedge is not a reason to keep filling hedges.

Closing. Zero point six percent. One hundred and thirty one uses. Three hundred and forty percent. Seven thousand jobs. Seventy percent. My opponent had a story about checkouts and a lot of questions. I had the findings. Policy should follow the numbers, and the numbers say no ban.

Weigh it. I explained why a free bag gets taken by reflex and why a charge stops that, which nobody disputed. I answered the cotton figure with what shoppers actually switched to, the bin liner figure with what it displaces, and jobs with where the same factories go. I asked what the five numbers measured and was given the five numbers again. A figure you cannot explain when asked is not evidence, it is a recitation. The mechanism was made and it was not met.

cases.motionEn: Homework should be banned in secondary schools
cases.motionNegEn: Homework should not be banned in secondary schools
cases.note: OFF-TOPIC, strong side AGAINST. FOR wanders: a story about a hated teacher, a rant about screens and phones, school lunches, a cousin who became a plumber, touching homework only in passing and never engaging the retention mechanism. AGAINST argues spaced practice with a mechanism, answers the inequality point (no quiet room at home) with a design fix, and names what FOR never engaged. A judge that credits fluent talking that is not about the motion picks FOR and fails; delivery is substance per second on topic.

lines.text: So I want to start with my year nine maths teacher, Mr Hollis, who I genuinely think hated children. He would set forty questions on a Friday, and you would spend your whole weekend on it, and he would not even mark it. And that is what I think of when I think of school. Honestly the whole system is broken, the lunches are terrible, they give them chips every day, and then everyone wonders why kids are tired. And the phones, kids are on their phones constantly, that is the real problem, not whether they did their worksheet.

The reason homework exists is a mechanism called spacing. If you meet an idea once in a lesson and never touch it again, most of it is gone in a week; if you meet it again a day later and then a few days after that, it sticks, and each return takes less time than the last. Homework is the cheapest way to create the second and third meeting, because a lesson can only hold the first. So the question is not whether forty unmarked questions are good, they are not, it is whether we should ban the only tool that puts the second meeting into a school week. Fix bad homework; do not ban homework.

My opponent talks about spacing, and that is all very scientific, but let me tell you about my cousin. He hated school, never did a single piece of homework, and he is a plumber now earning more than any of us, so what did homework ever do for him. And while we are on it, the amount of pressure on kids now is insane, the exams, the league tables, the uniforms, the whole thing is a machine. I saw a thing the other day about a school in Finland where they finish at two and have no homework and they are top of everything. Different world.

Two things in there were about homework, so let me take them. The cousin: one person who succeeded without homework is not evidence that homework does nothing, any more than one smoker who lived to ninety is evidence about smoking. The Finland point: Finnish schools do set homework, less of it, and they set it well, which is exactly my position. And the real objection to homework, which my opponent has not made but I will make for them so it can be answered, is inequality: the kid with a quiet room and a parent who can help gets more from it than the kid without. That is a reason to run a homework club in the school building after the last bell, which many schools do, not a reason to take the second meeting away from everyone.

To defend my case. It is one mechanism, spacing, and one comparison: what a school week looks like with a second meeting of each idea and without one. Without it, the lesson is the only meeting and the week is a series of first impressions. With it, done in twenty minutes, the idea is met again before it fades. Nothing said so far has touched that. Mr Hollis, the lunches, the phones and the cousin are all real things, and none of them is a reason to ban the second meeting.

Look, I just think childhood should be childhood. When I was a kid we were out on our bikes until it got dark, and now they are inside doing worksheets or on their phones, mostly on their phones, and I do not think that is healthy. My mum used to say school is for school and home is for home, and I think she had a point. And another thing, the teachers are exhausted, they are marking until midnight, and that is a whole other problem nobody talks about, the pay, the hours, the number of them leaving.

Closing. I gave you a mechanism, spacing, and why a lesson alone cannot provide it. I answered the cousin, answered Finland, and raised and answered the inequality objection myself because nobody else did. In four speeches the other side gave you a maths teacher, the lunches, the phones, a plumber, bikes until dark, and teacher pay. All of it may be true and none of it is about whether a second meeting with an idea should be banned. The case was made and it was never met.

In closing, I think what I have been saying all along is that we need to look at the bigger picture. The lunches, the phones, the pressure, the teachers leaving, my cousin who did fine. Kids need to be kids. My opponent had a lot to say about spacing and meetings, but at the end of the day I think most people know in their heart that childhood should not be a worksheet. Ban it.

cases.motionEn: Restaurants should be required to print calorie counts on menus
cases.motionNegEn: Restaurants should not be required to print calorie counts on menus
cases.note: LENGTH FALSE-POSITIVE TRAP, strong side FOR. The LONG side is the better one here: FOR speaks at length but every sentence does work, a distinct mechanism, a concrete example, or a direct answer, and it engages every AGAINST point. AGAINST is short and empty: slogans (nanny state, people know what they eat, it is just a number) with no mechanism and no engagement. A judge that has learned to discount length itself, rather than padding, picks AGAINST and fails. Length is not the fault; restatement is.

lines.text: Three reasons, each with a mechanism. First, information changes the choice only when it arrives at the moment of choosing: a calorie figure on a website nobody reads does nothing, a figure next to the price on the board does, because that is where the decision is made. Second, the bigger effect is not on the diner but on the kitchen: the day a chain has to print that its muffin is six hundred calories, the muffin gets reformulated to four hundred and fifty, because the number is now a marketing problem. Chains that had to label cut calories per item across the menu in the years afterward, mostly by quietly shrinking portions and swapping oils, without anyone ordering differently. Third, the cost of compliance is a spreadsheet, once per recipe, and the rule already exempts small independents in every version that has been passed. So the case is: the number moves the diner a little, moves the recipe a lot, and costs the restaurant almost nothing.

This is the nanny state. People know what they are eating. If you order a burger you know it is a burger. Adults do not need the government printing numbers on their dinner. It is just a number and it will not change anything.

Take each of those. People know what they are eating: they know it is a burger, they do not know that the salad with the dressing and the croutons has more calories than the burger, and in every survey where diners were asked to guess, they were off by a third or more on exactly those items, always in the same direction. That is the gap the number closes. It is a number that will not change anything: I gave you the mechanism by which it changes the recipe rather than the diner, and that has not been touched. Nanny state: a label is the opposite of a ban, it leaves every choice open and adds one fact next to the price, which is what we already do for alcohol percentage, allergens and the price itself. Nobody calls the price a nanny.

Nobody reads those numbers. Everyone knows a burger is unhealthy. This is just more red tape for restaurants that are already struggling, and it treats people like children. It is a number on a menu. It changes nothing.

I will keep it simple because it is simple. It is the nanny state, people can decide for themselves, and a number on a menu does not change what anyone orders. Restaurants have enough to deal with. Leave them alone.

Nobody reads the numbers is a claim about diners, and my main argument was never about diners. It is about the kitchen: the chain reformulates because the number is public, and the diner who never looks at the board still eats the smaller muffin. That is the point that has now been passed over three times. On red tape for struggling restaurants: the rule exempts independents below a size threshold, and a chain with a thousand outlets computes each recipe once. And on treating people like children: the alternative to giving an adult a fact is withholding it, and I do not see how withholding is the grown-up option.

In closing, this is the nanny state and people know what they are eating. A number on a menu changes nothing, nobody reads it, and restaurants do not need more rules. Leave people alone to enjoy their dinner.

Weigh what was answered. I gave three mechanisms: the moment of choice, the kitchen reformulating, and the near-zero cost with the small-business exemption. The reply was that nobody reads the number, which I answered with the kitchen, and nanny state, which I answered with the price tag and the allergen list we already print. The reformulation point was raised in my first sentence and never once engaged. Four short speeches said the same three slogans; the case against them was made in full and left standing.

cases.motionEn: Universities should abolish letter grades
cases.motionNegEn: Universities should keep letter grades
cases.note: CHATBOT-PASTE FALSE-POSITIVE TRAP, strong side AGAINST. AGAINST is polished, structured and fluent (signposting, numbered points, clean sentences) AND engages: it quotes back what FOR actually said each turn and answers it, with mechanisms. FOR is scrappy spoken English that never engages, repeating that grades are stressful and that it just feels wrong. The paste family is about engagement, not polish: a judge that has learned tidy prose means pasted text and penalizes it picks FOR and fails. Polish plus engagement is simply good debating.

lines.text: ok so, um, grades. I just think they are, like, really stressful, right, everyone is stressed all the time about their GPA, and it is not what learning is supposed to be about. Like you go to uni to learn and instead you are just chasing a letter. My mate basically had a breakdown over a B minus. So, yeah, I think we should get rid of them and just, like, let people learn.

Three points, and I will come back to each as the debate goes on. First, a grade is a signal that travels: an employer or a graduate school in another city cannot sit in on your seminars, so the letter is how your work reaches people who were not in the room. Remove it and they fall back on the name of the university, which is a far worse signal for anyone who did not attend a famous one. Second, feedback without a grade is feedback without a scale: a paragraph of comments tells you what to fix but not how far you are from the standard, and students consistently ask for both. Third, on the stress my opponent raised: the stress comes from the stakes, not from the letter. A pass-fail system with the same stakes moves the anxiety to the pass line; it does not remove it.

right, so, um, they said a lot of stuff about signals and whatever, but like, I still think it is about the stress. Everyone I know is stressed. And it is not real learning, it is memorising for the letter. Some unis do pass fail and they seem fine, like, I read about one. So I do not think the sky falls in. It just feels wrong that four years comes down to a letter.

Let me answer the two things that were actually said. Some universities run pass-fail and seem fine: the ones that do are almost all elite medical schools, where the admission itself is the signal and the residency match uses a separate exam score, which is to say they replaced the letter with a different number rather than with nothing. That is my first point in practice. Memorising for the letter: that is an argument about how courses are assessed, and the fix is better assessment, projects, open-book problems, not the removal of the scale the assessment reports on. And I note the travelling-signal point, the one about students from non-famous universities, has not been answered at all.

To defend my case, I will restate the mechanism precisely because it is the one thing the other side has not engaged. A grade is portable information. Without it, the person deciding whether to hire or admit you has two options: the reputation of your institution, or a costly interview process that most will not run for most applicants. Both favour the already-advantaged. The student a grade helps most is the first-in-family student at a mid-ranked university with a first-class transcript, and that is exactly the student a no-grade system makes invisible.

ok, um, so, I hear all that, but honestly I keep coming back to the same thing, it is just so stressful, and I do not think that is how it should be. Like, employers can just, I dunno, talk to people, interview them. And my mate with the B minus, that was not a signal, that was a bad week. So, yeah. It is stressful and it feels wrong, that is my case.

In closing, weigh the two cases. I offered a mechanism for what a grade does, portable information that protects the student without a famous name, and I answered pass-fail with what those schools actually replaced the letter with, memorising with better assessment, and stress with the point that stakes cause stress and a pass line has stakes too. The other side raised stress four times, a friend with a bad week, and one university it read about, and never engaged the signal point once. Employers can just talk to people was the only answer, and I explained why that favours the well-connected. Keep the grade.

so, closing, um, I think it is pretty simple. Grades are stressful, everyone knows it, and they are not what learning is about. My opponent had a lot of points about signals and employers, and fair enough, but like, I just think if you asked students they would say get rid of them. It feels wrong to me and I think it feels wrong to most people. So, get rid of them.

cases.motionEn: Daylight saving time should be abolished
cases.motionNegEn: Daylight saving time should be kept
cases.note: TONE FALSE-POSITIVE TRAP, strong side AGAINST. AGAINST is abrasive: it calls arguments lazy, tells the opponent to wake up, and lands one personal jab, but every sharp line is attached to an actual argument and it answers each FOR point with a mechanism. FOR is unfailingly courteous (respectfully, my learned opponent makes a fair point) and empty: confusion, farmers, and it feels unnecessary, never developed and never engaging. The adhom family is about substituting mockery for argument; here the rude side has the argument. A judge that scores manners picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Thank you, and I want to say at the outset how much I respect anyone willing to take the other side of this. My position is simply that daylight saving time is confusing and unnecessary. Twice a year everyone changes their clocks, people are tired, it was originally for farmers and even the farmers do not want it. I think most reasonable people would agree we could simply do without it, and I look forward to a respectful exchange.

Respectful exchange, fine, but let us have an actual argument first, because so far there is not one. Here is why the clock moves: people are awake and outside in the evening, not at five in the morning. An hour of light moved from before dawn, when nearly everyone is asleep, to after work, when people walk, shop, play sport and drive home, is an hour that is used instead of wasted. That is the whole mechanism. And the it was for farmers line is a myth that has been debunked so many times that repeating it is just lazy: farmers lobbied against it, it was introduced to save fuel in wartime, and it was kept because people liked evening light.

My learned opponent makes a fair point about evenings, and I would never dismiss it. But I would respectfully suggest that the confusion is real. People miss appointments, they arrive an hour early to church, computers have to be updated. And the tiredness the week after the spring change is well known. I think, on balance, and with great respect for the other view, simplicity should win.

Arrive an hour early to church is not a policy argument, it is an anecdote about one person who cannot read a calendar. Computers update themselves; that problem was solved twenty years ago. The tiredness the week after the spring change is the one real point in there, so I will actually answer it: it is one short night, once a year, and the honest comparison is against what you get instead. Abolish the change and you must pick one clock forever. Pick permanent standard time and the sun sets before four in the afternoon in winter for most of the country, which is the arrangement that was tried and reversed within a year because people hated leaving work in the dark. Pick permanent summer time and children walk to school in the dark in January. The change exists because neither fixed clock fits both halves of the year. My opponent has clearly never been outside at four in the afternoon in December.

Let me defend the case in one line and then wake my opponent up. The line: an hour of daylight is worth more after work than before dawn, and no fixed clock delivers that in both summer and winter. Now the wake-up: three speeches in, the case for abolishing consists of confusing, farmers, and simplicity. I have answered farmers with the history, confusing with the fact that phones do it for you, and the tiredness with what the alternative actually costs. Nothing has come back. Being polite about an empty case does not fill it.

I appreciate my opponent's passion, truly. I would only say, with respect, that many countries manage without changing their clocks and seem to do perfectly well, and that simplicity has a value of its own. I think reasonable people can disagree here. My case remains that the change is confusing and unnecessary, and I am content to let the audience weigh that.

Closing. Many countries manage without it: yes, the ones near the equator where day length barely changes, which is precisely why they do not need it, and the ones far from it that tried a fixed clock and went back. That was the point I made and it was met with reasonable people can disagree. Weigh it. One side gave you a mechanism, evening light is used and dawn light is not, the history of why it exists, and the cost of each fixed alternative. The other side gave you manners. Keep the clock change.

In closing, and I thank my opponent for a lively debate, I have said that the clock change is confusing, that it is unnecessary, and that simplicity matters. I would respectfully leave it there. I think most people, in their hearts, would rather not change their clocks twice a year, and I trust the audience to see it the same way.

cases.motionEn: Police traffic stops should be replaced by automated cameras
cases.motionNegEn: Police traffic stops should not be replaced by automated cameras
cases.note: CONCESSION OF THE MAJOR POINT, strong side AGAINST. Unlike concession-1 and -2, where the concession was minor and the conceder won, here FOR concedes the central point of the debate (a camera cannot stop a drunk or dangerous driver in the moment, which is the main safety purpose of a stop) and treats it as a detail. AGAINST builds on the concession with a mechanism and wins the clash; FOR never recovers it. The judge must weigh WHAT was conceded, not the act of conceding: a judge that has learned conceding is honest and rewards it regardless picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Traffic stops are the most common contact most people ever have with police, and they are where bias shows up most: who gets pulled over for a broken tail light depends on who is driving. A camera does not care who is driving. It photographs the plate at the same speed for everyone, sends the same fine, and frees officers for work that needs a person. Consistent, unbiased, and cheaper. Replace the stop.

A camera measures one thing: speed at a point, or a red light at a junction. It cannot tell that the car weaving between lanes at eleven at night has a drunk driver in it, and it cannot get that driver off the road before the crash. Impaired and dangerous driving is what stops are for, and impaired driving is behind roughly a third of road deaths. The fine arrives in the post three weeks later; the crash happens tonight. So the question is not whether cameras are fairer at speeding tickets, they are, it is whether you can remove the only tool that intervenes in real time.

I will grant that: a camera cannot pull over a drunk driver in the moment. Fine. But that is a small slice of stops. The vast majority of traffic stops are for speeding, equipment, registration, things a camera handles better and with no bias. So we replace the routine stop with the camera and we get consistency across millions of interactions. My opponent is arguing about the exception; I am arguing about the rule.

Notice what was just conceded and how quickly it was moved past. The one function only a stop can perform, taking a dangerous driver off the road before the crash, was granted and then called a small slice. It is a small slice of stops and a large slice of deaths, and that is the whole weighing. Nobody is defending a tail-light stop as a lifesaver; the point is that the officer who stops the tail light at eleven at night is the same officer who smells the alcohol. Take the stop away and the camera catches the speed and misses the driver. My opponent has given me the central point and asked to talk about the routine ones instead.

To defend the case and build on what was granted. The bias point is real and I will not wave it away: stops fall unevenly and that needs fixing. The fix is cameras for speed and lights, which I support, plus recorded, audited stops for the things a camera cannot do, which is where the concession bites. Replacing rather than supplementing removes the one intervention that happens before the crash. The other side agreed a camera cannot do that. Everything since has been about the paperwork stops, and paperwork was never the reason to keep the stop.

The drunk driving point is one point, and I addressed it: it is a minority of stops. The majority is where the bias is, and the majority is where the camera wins. Consistency, cost, no discretion for bias to hide in. I do not think a debate about millions of routine stops should be decided by the rare dramatic one. My case is about the rule.

Closing. The other side conceded that a camera cannot stop the driver who is about to kill someone, and then argued that this is rare. Rare in count and common in the death statistics is the whole reason stops exist. I agreed cameras for speed and lights, I agreed bias needs fixing, and I said how. What I will not agree is that the one tool that acts before the crash should go because most of its uses are boring. The central point was handed over in the first rebuttal and never taken back.

In closing: cameras are consistent, unbiased and cheap, and the routine stop is where bias lives. Yes, I said a camera cannot stop a drunk driver, and I stand by that being a small part of what stops do. The rule matters more than the exception. Replace the stop with the camera and millions of people get treated the same way for the first time.

cases.motionEn: Junk food advertising aimed at children should be banned
cases.motionNegEn: Junk food advertising aimed at children should not be banned
cases.note: DODGING THE STRONGEST POINT, strong side FOR. FOR's central point is a mechanism: children under about eight cannot tell an advert from the programme, so the parents-decide answer does not reach them, and the ad works precisely because it bypasses the decider. AGAINST never engages it: each turn it pivots to free speech, parental responsibility and where does it end, fluently, without once addressing the under-eights. FOR answers AGAINST's strongest point (the slippery slope on speech) directly with the tobacco and alcohol precedents. A judge that does not penalize the drop picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: Here is the mechanism the whole case rests on. Advertising to an adult is persuasion: you know it is an advert, you discount it. A child under about eight does not have that: developmental research consistently finds they cannot reliably tell where the cartoon ends and the advert begins, so to them the cereal is simply part of the show. That is not a loophole in parental choice, it is a bypass around it: the ad is designed to make the child ask, and the ask is aimed at a parent who did not get to see the ad. We already forbid advertising cigarettes and alcohol to children for exactly this reason. Add sugar-dense food.

This is a free speech question and a parenting question. Companies have a right to advertise a legal product, and parents have the responsibility to say no. If a child wants sugary cereal, the parent decides, that is what parents are for. And once you ban one category, where does it end: fizzy drinks today, then crisps, then cheese, then anything with fat in it. Governments should not be deciding what adverts a family sees.

Take the slippery slope first, because it is the best point on that side: the line already exists. Cigarettes and alcohol are legal products with a long-settled ban on advertising to children, and cheese has not followed, because the line is drawn at products where the harm is high and the audience cannot evaluate the claim. Now the part I most want answered: parents decide. My mechanism was that the under-eight cannot tell the ad from the show, so the ad reaches the child without passing through the parent at all. Parents decide answers the twelve-year-old. Who answers the five-year-old?

My opponent wants to talk about five-year-olds and I want to talk about principle. The principle is that adults, including parents, are responsible for what children consume, and the state is not. Every ban starts with a sympathetic case and ends with a bureaucracy deciding what counts as junk. Is a granola bar junk? Is orange juice? The moment you draw the line you have a committee, and the committee will keep drawing. Parental responsibility is the only line that does not move.

To defend the case: commercial speech is speech, and restricting it should require an extraordinary reason. Sugar is not cigarettes. Every family has a television and every family has a parent who can turn it off or say no at the shop. My opponent keeps returning to how children perceive adverts, and I would just say that the answer to a child's perception is a parent's judgement. That is what has always worked and it is what should keep working.

A parent's judgement is the answer to the child's perception: that sentence is the closest the other side has come to my point, and it is still not an answer, because the parent's judgement is exactly what the advert is designed to route around. The five-year-old does not perceive an advert and consult a parent; the five-year-old perceives part of the show and then asks, in the aisle, twenty times. The parent can say no, and the ban is about whether a company should be allowed to manufacture that ask in a mind that cannot see it coming. On the committee: we already have one, it draws the line for alcohol adverts, and it has not reached cheese in fifty years.

In closing, this is about who decides: parents or the state. I have said free speech, I have said parental responsibility, and I have said where does it end, and I stand by all three. My opponent had a lot of research about small children, and I have said what I think about that, which is that parents are the answer. Keep the state out of the advert break.

Weigh what was engaged. Their best point, the slope, I answered with the alcohol line that has held for fifty years. Their parents-decide point I showed does not reach the child the ad is aimed at, because the child cannot see the ad as an ad. That mechanism was raised in my first sentence and in every speech since, and the reply each time was principle, committee, and parents, none of which says how a five-year-old tells the cereal from the cartoon. A case that will not face the strongest point against it should not win.

cases.motionEn: Tap water is better than bottled water
cases.motionNegEn: Bottled water is better than tap water
cases.note: CONFIDENCE FALSE-POSITIVE TRAP, strong side FOR. FOR is assertive and blunt (this is not close, it is settled) AND substantive: municipal testing frequency versus bottling plants, the cost ratio with a mechanism, where bottled water often comes from, and direct answers to the taste and Flint points. AGAINST hedges constantly (I think, maybe, I am not sure, I have heard) AND is empty: taste, things about pipes, probably safer, never developed and never engaging. The confidence family is about certainty substituting for content; here the certain side has the content. A judge that has learned to reward hedging as honesty, or to dock assertiveness, picks AGAINST and fails.

lines.text: This one is not close, and I will show you why rather than just say so. Municipal water in most developed countries is tested many times a day at the plant and again in the distribution network, with results published, because a fault affects a whole city at once and everyone would know. A bottling plant is inspected on a schedule that is measured in months and its results are not published. So the water that is watched more closely is the one from the tap. Add that a large share of bottled water is municipal water that was filtered, put in plastic and sold at around a thousand times the price, and that the plastic is the single largest source of the bottle litter in rivers, and the case is settled: the tap is safer by supervision, cheaper by three orders of magnitude, and cleaner for the river.

I mean, I think bottled is probably better, I am not totally sure, but it tastes nicer, I think, most people would say that. And I have heard things about pipes, like old pipes, lead maybe, and there was that town in America, so tap might not be as safe as people think. I could be wrong. It just seems like bottled is more, I do not know, controlled, probably.

Two things were said, so I will answer both properly. Taste: the taste most people notice in tap water is chlorine, which is there precisely because it keeps the water safe between the plant and your kitchen, and it leaves in ten minutes in an open jug or instantly through a cheap filter. Bottled water has no chlorine because it does not travel through pipes, not because it is purer. The town in America: Flint was a real failure, and it was detected because municipal water is tested and the results are public; the scandal was that officials sat on the results, not that nobody had them. A bottling plant with the same fault would have had no public results to sit on. Lead pipes are a real issue in old housing and the answer is a filter certified for lead, which costs less than a month of bottles.

Yeah, I mean, that is probably fair about the chlorine, I think. I still sort of feel like bottled is safer though, maybe, because it is sealed, I suppose. And people do buy a lot of it, so there must be something to it, I would have thought. I am not an expert. It is hard to say really.

So, to defend my side, I would just say, I think, that it comes down to what people prefer, and a lot of people prefer bottled, and there is probably a reason for that. It might be the taste, it might be the safety thing, I am not sure which. I do not think tap is bad exactly, I just think bottled is maybe a bit better, on the whole, probably.

Sealed is the new point, so here is the answer: a sealed bottle stored in a warm warehouse or a hot car leaches compounds from the plastic into the water over weeks, which is a risk the tap does not have at all, because the tap has no shelf life. And people buy a lot of it so there must be something to it: people bought a lot of cigarettes too. Purchases measure marketing, not quality. I have given you supervision, price, the river, chlorine, Flint, lead and the plastic itself. The reply so far has been I think, probably, and maybe. I am confident because the mechanisms are simple and they all point one way.

In closing, I think, I mean, I am not certain, but I still lean bottled. It tastes nicer to me, it is sealed, and a lot of people choose it. My opponent had a lot of points and they were probably good ones, I am not sure I can answer all of them. But that is my view, I think.

Weigh it. One side explained who tests the water and how often, why it costs a thousand times less, why the taste difference is chlorine and how to remove it, what Flint actually shows, and what plastic does to sealed water in a warm room. The other side said it probably tastes nicer and people buy a lot of it. I was blunt because the case is strong, and being blunt about a strong case is not the same as being loud about an empty one. Tap.

cases.motionEn: Personal finance should be a required course in secondary schools
cases.motionNegEn: Personal finance should not be a required course in secondary schools
cases.note: REPETITION VS DEVELOPMENT, strong side AGAINST, and the intuitive position is FOR so this also tests neutrality. FOR has one point, kids need to know about money, and says it four times with different examples of things kids do not know, never developing it, never engaging. AGAINST develops a case across the turns: the fixed-hours cost, the decay mechanism (taught at sixteen, needed at twenty-six), what happened where it was mandated, a better alternative (just-in-time and embedded in maths), and a direct answer to FOR. A judge that scores a slogan repeated as a case sustained picks FOR and fails.

lines.text: Kids leave school knowing the quadratic formula and not knowing what a credit score is. That is absurd. They do not know how a mortgage works, they do not know what compound interest does to a credit card balance, they do not know how to read a payslip. Money is the one thing every single one of them will have to deal with every day of their adult life. Teach it, and make it required, because the kids who need it most are the ones who would not choose it.

I agree people should understand money; the question is whether a required course at sixteen is how they come to. Two mechanisms say no. First, school hours are fixed, so a required course displaces something, and it is usually the option subjects that keep some students in school at all. Second, and this is the bigger one, skills decay when they are not used: a sixteen-year-old taught mortgages will not touch a mortgage for ten years, and by then the products, the rates and the rules have changed, and the lesson is a faint memory. The places that mandated a course and then measured behaviour a few years later mostly found no difference in saving, borrowing or credit scores. What did work was teaching the thing at the moment it was needed: a short module before a student takes out a loan, a payslip walkthrough in the first job.

My opponent says kids will forget. But they need to know this. They need to know what an interest rate is. They need to know that a payday loan will eat them alive. They need to know what a pension is before they opt out of one at twenty two. This is basic. It is money. Everyone needs it. Make it required.

They need to know is a statement I agree with, and it is not an argument for a required course at sixteen; it is an argument for knowing, and the debate is about the mechanism that delivers it. I gave you two problems, the displaced hours and the decay, and the reply was a list of things people should know, which I also think they should know. So let me build the alternative properly. Compound interest already sits in the maths curriculum; teach it with a credit card statement instead of an abstract example and the concept lands with no extra hours. Payday loans and pensions belong in a two-hour module delivered by employers and universities at the point of the first job or the first loan, which is when it is remembered because it is immediately used.

Defending the case and adding one more piece. The strongest version of the other side is the one they have not made: the kids who most need it will not get a first-job module because their first job does not offer one. Fair, and the answer is the embedded route, the credit card in the maths lesson and the payslip in the careers session, which reaches everyone without a new required course. So the choice is not teach money or do not; it is a standalone course that decays before it is used, against the same content placed where it is used. My two mechanisms and the measured results have not been answered.

I will say it again because it is the whole point: kids need to know about money. They do not know what a credit score is. They do not know what APR means. They do not know how tax works. A course would fix that. It is the most important subject they could take and it is the one subject we do not require. That is backwards.

Closing. I gave you the hours cost, the decay mechanism, what happened where courses were mandated, and an alternative that puts the same content where it is used and reaches everyone. Across four speeches the other side told you kids need to know about money, with a fresh list each time, and never once engaged decay, the measured results, or the embedded alternative. Wanting the outcome is not the same as arguing for the method. The mechanism was made and it was not met.

In closing: kids need to know about money. Credit scores, interest, mortgages, payslips, pensions, tax. My opponent had theories about forgetting, but you do not forget what matters, and nothing matters more than money. Make it required.
